title: A Orchard for the Letter
premise: In 1918, on a fog-bound Pacific coast, Bram Sterling has spent ten years as an indentured clerk for the Meridian Trading Company, learning that survival means silence. When census taker Odile Voss arrives to count the harbor's people and asks about a diver who drowned under suspicious circumstances years ago, Bram's careful lies begin to unravel — and she discovers the company's ledgers hide the truth of her father's death. Racing an armistice that will dissolve the company's wartime charter and burn its records, Bram and Odile must copy out the evidence before the workshop is torched. In the end, Bram chooses truth over loyalty, testifies at the inquiry, and plants a pear tree where the workshop stood.
about_author: Beatrix Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping manifests from coastal trading towns. She writes historical fiction about the people history forgot to count.

chapters.title: The Counting Season
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The census taker Odile Voss arrives at Meridian's harbor office, and Bram, now head clerk, is ordered to manage her. Bram performs the fluent half-truths of her trade, but Odile's questions are precise in ways that unsettle her. Emotional beat: the uneasy comfort of old habits beginning to crack.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Odile asks who owned the dive boat Pearl Lark the night it sank with four men aboard, including a diver named Sterling. Bram lies smoothly — then finds her own childhood name in a ledger she was never meant to read. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground of her loyalty shifts.

chapters.title: What the Ledgers Keep
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Working late in the counting house, Odile cross-references manifests and finds insurance payouts signed by men who never existed. She suspects Bram knows more than she says. Emotional beat: the loneliness of an outsider whose only ally may be lying to her.

chapters.title: The Diver's Daughter
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram visits her mother's grave and remembers her father teaching her to hold her breath, to read water, to keep quiet. She confronts the foreman Hask, who warns her that the armistice will come and everything will be 'settled.' Emotional beat: grief sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: A Debt in Ink
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Bram offers Odile a bargain: her testimony for protection from the company's reprisals. They begin copying pages by lamplight after hours. Hask grows suspicious; a clerk disappears. Emotional beat: two wary women building trust out of mutual need.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. News spreads that peace terms may be signed within weeks, which will void Meridian's wartime charter and trigger destruction of its records. The company accelerates 'inventory audits.' Bram realizes the workshop itself will be burned. Emotional beat: the clock becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: Hask's Hand
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Hask catches Bram in the archive and gives her a choice: sign a false deposition clearing the company, or lose her indenture papers and be turned out with nothing. Bram signs — and hates herself. Emotional beat: the cost of survival measured against the self she wants to be.

chapters.title: Night Copyists
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The final copying: Bram steals the master ledger while Odile distracts the night watch. A fire breaks out in the drying loft — set or accidental, no one can say. They escape with the pages as the workshop burns behind them. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. At the harbor inquiry, Bram testifies despite her false deposition, naming the men who scuttled the Pearl Lark for the insurance money. Her words hang in a room full of company men. Emotional beat: the trembling courage of choosing truth when loyalty would be easier.

chapters.title: A Orchard for the Letter
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, months later. The inquiry convicts two officers; the rest scatter. Freed of her indenture, Bram receives her father's last letter, held ten years in the company mail room. She reads it standing in the ashes' footprint, then plants a pear sapling there. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace — memory kept, justice partial, life continuing.
